did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a trumpet blast in Zion and the announcement that the day of the Lord is near, calling the inhabitants of the land to fear and pay attention.
Did you know? The day of the Lord is described as a day of darkness, clouds, and thick darkness, while an immense army unlike any seen in previous or future generations is also described.
Did you know? The army is portrayed as a destructive force: before it, the land looks like the Garden of Eden, but behind it, it becomes a desolate wilderness.
Did you know? The army’s members move swiftly and in orderly formation: each one marches along his own path, and no one deviates from his course.
Did you know? The description of the day of the Lord also includes cosmic upheaval: the earth trembles, the heavens shake, and the sun, moon, and stars lose their light.
Did you know? Alongside the description of disaster, the Lord calls the people to return to him with all their heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning.

Did you know? The prophet emphasizes that repentance must be inward: “Tear your hearts and not your garments”; this call is grounded in the description of the Lord as gracious, compassionate, and abounding in steadfast love.
Did you know? The trumpet is used again as a call to the entire community: to consecrate a fast, summon a solemn assembly, and gather all the people.
Did you know? The priests pray between the portico and the altar, asking the Lord to have mercy on his people so that they will not be handed over to disgrace among the nations.

Did you know? After announcing that the devastation of the land has been removed, the people of Zion are called to rejoice, and the Lord promises rain—the early and late rains—as well as abundant grain, wine, and olive oil.
